Art car v2 — design notebook

Working document for the custom electric chassis and Selina's nine body concepts. Everything with a number in it is an estimate unless it cites a source; the sketch dimensions in the volumetric study are read off the renderings by eye and are meant to be edited.

1. Fixed constraints

Transport

U-Haul 6×12 utility trailer with ramp
Inside deck 11′11″ × 6′ (143″ × 72″). Ramp opening 4′9″ (57″). Rail height 2′6″. Empty 2,290 lb, max load 3,710 lb, ramp rated 1,810 lb. Max 55 mph.
Cruise America 30′ (C30)
Receiver hitch, customer supplies tow gear. Contract limit: towing weight within 2,500 lb, daily towing charge. RV is 8.3′ wide.
Weight. The current rig already runs well past Cruise America's 2,500 lb warranty: ramp trailer 2,290 lb empty plus a ~1,000 lb Taylor-Dunn, plywood body, a couple of e-bikes and four 12 V batteries. So the number that actually governs is the trailer's own rating — 3,710 lb of load, 1,810 lb on the ramp — and whatever the RV's hitch and brakes tolerate. A new chassis at ~1,000–1,200 lb (steel platform, 15 kWh pack, four motor corners) before body, cargo and bikes is roughly where the current load sits, so the budget is "no heavier than today" rather than "lighter."
  • Ramp width 57″ is the hard width limit for anything that rolls on under its own power. Wider decks need the roof and side panels to come off, or a pair of separate ramps and a 72″ limit.
  • Roof structures must be demountable regardless; nothing in the sketches fits on an open trailer assembled.
  • Height on the highway: 13′6″ legal, trailer deck ~24″ off the ground, so ~11′ of stack is available — wind load is the real limit long before that.

Chassis envelope

  • Maximum 54″ × 120″ (4.5′ × 10′). Three inches of clearance on the ramp, 23″ short of the trailer deck. The chassis can be smaller in either dimension; the body can extend past it on any side. Everything the passengers sit on is body, cantilevered or supported off this rectangle.
  • Wheels live inside the envelope, so track ≈ 48–50″ and wheelbase ≈ 80–100″. Every inch of body outboard of the track is lever arm against the chassis mass.

Playa

  • Mutant vehicle licensing: radically modified appearance, conventional steering preferred, 5 mph at night / 10 mph day, lit perimeter after dark.
  • Surface: hardpan with ruts, dust drifts, and occasional wet patches. Low-speed, high-torque, dust everywhere. Anything unsealed dies.
  • Field service: any single corner (wheel + motor + suspension) must be swappable with a jack, a wrench, and two connectors.

2. Chassis concept

  • Platform. Welded steel rectangle. Battery box is the central mass, mounted low. Roof loads go through a central spine or mast into the battery box, not through the side panels.
  • Drive. Four independent 48 V motors, one per corner, used for traction and torque split. Not skid steer.
  • Steering. Ackermann on the front pair (or all four) via knuckles. Independent motors don't need to do the steering.
  • Corner module. Trailing arm carrying a 12″ direct-drive hub motor, air spring above. All four identical apart from the front steering knuckle; carry one spare. (See section 3.)
  • Suspension. Airbags preferred: kneel for boarding, level on ruts, adjust ride height for the trailer ramp.
  • Bus voltage. 48 V for everything on the drive side; 12 V rails per lighting zone via DC-DC. Golf cart / marine / e-scooter parts ecosystem.

3. Corner module

Each corner is one bolt-on unit: a 12″ direct-drive hub motor in a trailing arm, an air spring above it, one phase/hall connector and one air line. Front corners add a steering knuckle. Carry one complete spare.

PartPickEach×4Notes
Motor + wheelQS205 12″ hub, 3 kW rated, 150 N·m peak, 48 V winding$300–600$1,300–2,400~$300 direct from QS (10–12 wk), $500–630 US eBay stock. Needs ~40 N·m per wheel at 5 mph fully loaded, so it loafs. Ask for the low-speed winding.
Controller48 V sine-wave FOC, 80 A (Sabvoton / Fardriver / Kelly)$120–250$500–1,000One per motor for torque split. CAN or serial out so a small board can read speed/current per corner.
Air springAir Lift Dominator D2500, 294–2,096 lb, 7.7″ stroke$111$450D2600 if corner loads exceed ~1,500 lb. Never plumb left/right together.
Air management12 V compressor, 2 gal tank, 4 solenoid valves, 4 pressure sensors$400–600Per-corner pressure = per-corner load; this is the tip-over warning.
Arm, knuckle, brackets, steelWelded, 2 fixed rear, 2 steered front$300–500Route phase wires through the steering pivot on the front pair.
Total~$3,000–5,000

Why direct-drive hubs and not a geared motor: a 4,300 rpm go-kart motor needs ~50:1 of reduction to turn a 20″ wheel at 5 mph. AGV and forklift drive units have the right torque and ratio but come with 8″ polyurethane wheels and top out around 2 mph; electric-tractor motors are 10–30 kW industrial units. A 16-pole-pair outrunner hub motor is the same idea as a tractor traction motor — many poles, lots of copper, high torque at low rpm — already packaged in a wheel with a tire that works on dirt.

Tipping threshold

Static roll-over about the outside tire, worst case: every passenger on one side, nobody on the other. Chassis mass on the centerline at the track half-width; passengers at 200 lb each with their centroid 10″ inboard of the platform rim. Air springs change none of this — they level the deck and measure the load, but the moment balance is pure geometry.

Reads as: how many 200 lb adults can sit on one rim before the inside wheels unload. Below ~4 is uncomfortable once a wheel drops into a rut. Chassis mass includes the pack. The 74″ track row assumes 12″ bolt-on spacers or outrigger stubs fitted on the playa and removed for the ramp.

4. Battery

Decision: new LiFePO4 prismatic cells, 16S per string, two independent strings. Used EV modules were considered and set aside — see below.

EVE LF280K (3.2 V / 280 Ah, ~0.9 kWh, 5.4 kg, 174 × 72 × 207 mm)

15 kWh (16 cells)30 kWh (32)45 kWh (48)
Cells (US-landed, ~$66–100 each)~$1,300~$2,600~$3,900
BMS, busbars, fusing, contactors, enclosure~$700~$1,000~$1,300
DIY total~$2,000~$3,600~$5,200
Turnkey 48 V packs (~$200–300/kWh)$3–4.5k$6–9k$9–13k
Cell weight / packaged86 kg / ~100 kg173 / ~200 kg260 / ~300 kg
Cell volume / packaged41 L / ~55 L83 / ~110 L125 / ~165 L
Box (2 deep × 8 long per layer)~23 × 14 × 9 in~46 × 14 × 9 in~46 × 21 × 9 in
Continuous power (0.5 C, V3 cells)~7 kW~14 kW~21 kW
  • Peak power scales with parallel strings, not just range: a single 16S string tops out around 7 kW continuous, which is tight for four motors in soft playa with ten aboard.
  • Two independent strings with their own BMS give redundancy — one trips, limp home on the other.
  • 314 Ah cells now sell at the same per-cell price, so ~33 kWh for the 30 kWh money.
  • Battery mass is smaller than intuition: even 45 kWh is ~300 kg, about the weight of the steel frame. Low and flat is what helps the CG; it won't be the dominant mass.

The only Leaf configuration worth a second look is a whole salvage 24 kWh pack at ~$1,000–1,500 with a tested state of health, reconfigured 7S6P (~13 kWh real) as a drive-only pack with a separate small LFP bank for lights. Otherwise new cells win on price, weight, volume, heat tolerance, and known lifespan.

5. Core shapes on the base

With the chassis fixed at 54″ × 120″, the body question reduces to how the seating platform hangs off that rectangle. Selina's five options, drawn at one scale with the base (solid) and trailer deck (dashed):

  • Round. 33″ of cantilever all the way round, but evenly, so the platform is a ring beam on a central mast and nothing is worse than anything else. Every seat is outboard of the track, which is where the roll question lives.
  • Long. Zero sideways cantilever, 40″ off each end. The safest for stability and the closest to today's car — and today's problem: it overhangs the trailer by 4–5 ft.
  • Wide. Doubling the width puts 27″ of cantilever each side if centered, 54″ if hung off one side. Sideways cantilever is the expensive direction, so this one wants a bolt-on outrigger axle for playa or it's really a different chassis.
  • Cloverleaf. Four lobes, ~40″ beyond the base in every direction. The most seating for the envelope and the most demountable — each lobe is a module — but the widest thing to store and the hardest to keep the rail continuous.
  • Pods. Six 48″ two-seaters, 24″ past the sides and 28″ past the ends — the biggest six that fit without overlapping. Smallest cantilever of the "wide" options, every seat is a unit that comes off, and the driver takes one pod.

Rough mapping to the renderings: 1, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7 are Long (some drift toward Wide); 8 and 9 are Round; 2 is Pods; Cloverleaf is new and closest in spirit to 3.

7. Transport and assembly (working)

Direction under consideration: the car travels as modules, each light enough to roll on and off the trailer by hand or winch, and gets assembled at camp. The battery is its own rolling unit that goes under the car and bolts up to the frame.

ModuleTarget weightMoves howNotes
Chassis (frame, 4 corners, steering, controllers)≤ 800 lbDrives itself up the ramp on a small "get on the trailer" pack, or winchedFits 54″ × 120″. Stays in one piece — the joints in a split frame cost weight and stiffness.
Battery sled (30 kWh, BMS, contactors, DC-DC)~450–500 lbRolls on its own cart; positioned under the car centrelineCar kneels onto it (airbags) or the cart lifts (scissor/hydraulic); four bolts, two Anderson SB350 plugs, one comms plug. Also lets the pack charge at home off the car.
Seating modules (pods / lobes / benches)≤ 150 lb eachDollies, two peopleEach with its own rail and LED zone; one connector per module.
Roof / arches / mast≤ 60 lb per pieceStacked flat on the trailerSame demount logic as the current hoops.
  • The ramp is rated 1,810 lb; nothing should approach it. The 3,710 lb trailer load is the sum, and it's roughly what goes on today.
  • The ramp is ~20° when the deck is 24″ up. Pushing 500 lb up it is ~170 lb of force plus rolling resistance; a $100 12 V winch on the trailer tongue makes the cart and the dollies a one-person job.
  • Small casters sink in playa. Cart and dollies want 8–10″ pneumatic or solid wheels, and a couple of sheets of plywood to roll on at camp.
  • Hot-connecting a 48 V pack needs a precharge circuit in the sled so the plug doesn't arc into the controller capacitors.

8. Open questions

  • Round platform with a central mast (2, 8, 9) vs rectangle with a spine (the rest) — this decides track, wheelbase and how the roof comes apart for transport.
  • Does the base need to fit the 57″ ramp with its own power, or is the plan to winch it up on separate ramps?
  • Target passenger count. The sketches range from 8 to 14.
